A History of Ancient Egypt Page 3 1. The Gift of the Nile: Land and People Ancient Egypt was one of the longest-lived civilisations in human history. From the unification of the Nile Valley around 3100 BCE to the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BCE, a span of roughly three thousand years, the Egyptians developed a distinctive culture that left its mark on architecture, religion, writing, art and statecraft. To place this duration in perspective, the time that separates Cleopatra from the building of the Great Pyramid is greater than the time that separates Cleopatra from the present day.

The Greek historian Herodotus, who visited Egypt in the fifth century BCE, famously described the country as the gift of the Nile, and although the phrase is a simplification, it captures the central truth that the river made everything else possible. The Nile flows northward for more than 6,600 kilometres from its sources in the African highlands to the Mediterranean Sea, and in Egypt it cuts a narrow green ribbon through an otherwise arid landscape.

The Nile flows northward for more than 6,600 kilometres from its sources in the African highlands to the Mediterranean Sea, and in Egypt it cuts a narrow green ribbon through an otherwise arid landscape. The Egyptians themselves recognised this contrast and called their homeland Kemet, the Black Land, after the dark fertile silt left by the flood, while they called the surrounding desert Deshret, the Red Land. Most of the population lived within a few kilometres of the river, in a valley that is seldom more than twenty kilometres wide, and in the broad triangular Delta where the river divides into several branches before reaching the sea.

Most of the population lived within a few kilometres of the river, in a valley that is seldom more than twenty kilometres wide, and in the broad triangular Delta where the river divides into several branches before reaching the sea. The country was traditionally divided into Upper Egypt, the southern valley, and Lower Egypt, the northern Delta, and this duality remained fundamental to the way kings presented themselves for the whole of Egyptian history, as rulers of the Two Lands. The rhythm of life was set by the annual inundation.

The rhythm of life was set by the annual inundation. Each summer, rains in the Ethiopian highlands swelled the river, and from roughly June to September the floodwaters spread across the valley floor, depositing fresh silt and soaking the soil. When the water receded, farmers sowed their seed in the damp earth, and the crops grew over the following months until the harvest in the spring. The Egyptians divided the year into three seasons based on this cycle, named Akhet, the flood, Peret, the emergence or growing season, and Shemu, the harvest, as shown in Figure 1.1. A good flood meant plentiful grain and a prosperous state,

The desert on either side of the valley provided protection from invasion and a rich supply of resources. The eastern desert contained gold, copper and a variety of semi-precious stones, while the western desert held oases that served as outposts and trading centres. To the south, the cataracts of the Nile, rapids that made navigation difficult, formed a natural boundary between Egypt and the land of Nubia, and to the north the Mediterranean limited access by sea.

This relative isolation allowed Egyptian civilisation to develop with a high degree of continuity, although the Egyptians were never entirely cut off from their neighbours and traded actively with Nubia, the Levant, the Aegean and the Land of Punt, a region on the Red Sea coast that supplied incense, ebony and exotic animals. The river was also the main highway.

The river was also the main highway. Because the Nile flows north and the prevailing wind blows south, boats could drift downstream with the current and sail upstream with the wind, which made transport of people, grain and heavy stone remarkably efficient. This ease of movement helped to unify the country politically and made it possible to transport the enormous blocks of granite from Aswan that were used in temples and royal monuments. It is no coincidence that the Egyptian hieroglyph for travelling south shows a boat with a sail, while the sign for travelling north shows a boat without one.

Predynastic Egypt and the Unification of the Two Lands Human presence in the Nile Valley goes back hundreds of thousands of years, but the story of Egyptian civilisation begins in earnest in the Neolithic period. Around 5500 BCE, communities in the Fayum and in Upper Egypt began to herd cattle, sheep and goats and to cultivate wheat and barley, crops that had spread from the Near East. As the Sahara became progressively drier from about 5000 BCE onward, people from the surrounding regions moved toward the river, and this concentration of population in the valley was one of the preconditions for the emergence of a complex society.

The Predynastic period is divided by archaeologists into cultural phases named after the sites where they were first identified, such as Badari, Naqada and Maadi. The Naqada culture, which flourished in Upper Egypt from about 4000 to 3100 BCE, is particularly important.

The Naqada culture, which flourished in Upper Egypt from about 4000 to 3100 BCE, is particularly important. Over the course of these centuries, cemeteries show a growing difference in wealth between burials, with some individuals interred in large tombs filled with fine pottery, stone vessels, copper objects and imported goods such as lapis lazuli from Afghanistan. At sites like Hierakonpolis, Naqada and Abydos, local chiefs emerged who controlled trade and agricultural surplus, and the earliest signs of royal ideology, such as the motif of a ruler smiting enemies, begin to appear on decorated objects.

The process by which these regional centres were joined into a single state is only partly understood. Later Egyptian tradition credited a king called Menes with uniting the country and founding the capital at Memphis, near the point where the Delta meets the valley.

Later Egyptian tradition credited a king called Menes with uniting the country and founding the capital at Memphis, near the point where the Delta meets the valley. Modern scholars usually identify Menes with either King Narmer or King Hor-Aha, and the Narmer Palette, a carved slate object found at Hierakonpolis, is often interpreted as a commemoration of a victory over northern enemies. On one side the king wears the white crown of Upper Egypt, and on the other he wears the red crown of Lower Egypt, symbolising the political unification, although it is likely that the process of consolidation unfolded over several generations rather than in a single campaign.

A History of Ancient Egypt Page 7 The first two dynasties, known as the Early Dynastic Period, saw the consolidation of state institutions. The kings were buried at Abydos in large mud-brick tombs surrounded by the graves of retainers, and officials began to be buried in mastaba tombs at Saqqara, the cemetery of the new capital. During this period hieroglyphic writing developed from a collection of labels and symbols into a full system capable of recording the Egyptian language. Administration was organised through a bureaucracy of scribes who collected taxes in grain and labour, and the country was divided into administrative districts that the Greeks later called nomes.

The ideological foundations of kingship were also laid in this period. The king was regarded as the earthly embodiment of the god Horus, and on his death he was identified with Osiris, the god of the afterlife, while his successor became the new Horus. The royal titulary, a set of names that each king adopted, expressed different aspects of his role, and by the end of the Old Kingdom it comprised five names, including the birth name enclosed in a cartouche.

This concept of divine kingship, in which the ruler was responsible for maintaining Maat, the cosmic order of truth and justice, remained the central pillar of Egyptian political thought for the next three thousand years. The administrative skills developed in this formative period would soon be applied on a staggering scale in the construction of the first monumental stone buildings in the world.

The Old Kingdom: The Age of the Pyramids The Old Kingdom, covering the Third to the Sixth Dynasties from about 2686 to 2181 BCE, is often called the Age of the Pyramids. Its first great ruler, Djoser of the Third Dynasty, ordered the construction of a funerary complex at Saqqara designed by his chancellor Imhotep, who is remembered by later generations as an architect, physician and sage. Instead of the traditional mud-brick mastaba, Imhotep built a tomb of cut limestone with six successive levels, producing the Step Pyramid, which rises to about 62 metres and is the earliest large stone building known.

Instead of the traditional mud-brick mastaba, Imhotep built a tomb of cut limestone with six successive levels, producing the Step Pyramid, which rises to about 62 metres and is the earliest large stone building known. The complex included courtyards, chapels and dummy buildings that allowed the king to enjoy the festivals of the afterlife for eternity. The Fourth Dynasty marks the high point of pyramid building. Sneferu, the founder of the dynasty, built at least three major pyramids, including the Bent Pyramid and the Red Pyramid at Dahshur.

Sneferu, the founder of the dynasty, built at least three major pyramids, including the Bent Pyramid and the Red Pyramid at Dahshur. The Bent Pyramid has an unusual shape because the builders changed the angle of the walls from about 54 degrees to about 43 degrees halfway up, probably because of structural problems, while the Red Pyramid, with its constant lower angle, was the first true smooth-sided pyramid. These experiments provided the technical knowledge that made the Great Pyramid of Giza possible. Sneferu's son Khufu, called Cheops by the Greeks, built the Great Pyramid at Giza around 2560 BCE.

Sneferu's son Khufu, called Cheops by the Greeks, built the Great Pyramid at Giza around 2560 BCE. The structure originally stood about 146.6 metres high and was constructed from an estimated 2.3 million blocks of limestone, with granite beams used for the roofs of the internal chambers. It remained the tallest man-made structure in the world for nearly four thousand years. The discovery in 2013 of the Wadi al-Jarf papyri, the diary of an official called Merer, gave direct evidence of how limestone from the Tura quarries was transported by boat to Giza during Khufu's reign.

The workers who built the pyramid were not slaves, as popular legend long held, but paid labourers who were housed, fed and buried in tombs near the monuments. By the Fifth Dynasty pyramids became smaller and less well built, but their burial chambers began to be inscribed with the Pyramid Texts, the oldest known religious writings in the world, a collection of spells intended to help the dead king ascend to the sky and join the gods. The growing importance of the sun god Ra in this period is reflected in the building of sun temples and in the inclusion of Ra in the royal titulary.

The growing importance of the sun god Ra in this period is reflected in the building of sun temples and in the inclusion of Ra in the royal titulary. The Old Kingdom state was highly centralised. A vizier served as the king's chief minister, supervising the treasury, the judiciary and the building projects, and a network of provincial governors collected taxes and organised labour. Over time,

A History of Ancient Egypt Page 10 however, the system began to change. The king granted land and tax exemptions to temples and to officials, and provincial governors, called nomarchs, gradually made their offices hereditary and developed independent power bases. The reign of Pepi II of the Sixth Dynasty, which according to tradition lasted more than ninety years, was followed by the collapse of central authority. Climate change, a series of low Nile floods and political fragmentation combined to bring the Old Kingdom to an end around 2181 BCE.

The First Intermediate Period and the Middle Kingdom The period that followed the Old Kingdom, from about 2181 to 2055 BCE, is called the First Intermediate Period. Egyptian texts of later centuries describe it as a time of chaos, hunger and social upheaval, and some, like the Admonitions of Ipuwer, lament that the poor had become rich and the rich had become poor. Modern research has shown that the picture is more nuanced: provincial centres flourished, local art developed new styles, and nomarchs recorded their efforts to feed their people during famines.

Modern research has shown that the picture is more nuanced: provincial centres flourished, local art developed new styles, and nomarchs recorded their efforts to feed their people during famines. Nevertheless, the absence of a strong central authority meant that the country was divided between rival dynasties, one based at Heracleopolis in the north and another at Thebes in the south. The conflict was resolved by Mentuhotep II of the Eleventh Dynasty, a Theban king who reunified Egypt around 2055 BCE after a long struggle against the northern rulers.

The conflict was resolved by Mentuhotep II of the Eleventh Dynasty, a Theban king who reunified Egypt around 2055 BCE after a long struggle against the northern rulers. He built a remarkable mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, on the west bank of the Nile opposite Thebes, which later served as inspiration for Queen Hatshepsut's famous temple next door. His reunification inaugurated the Middle Kingdom, a period that the Egyptians themselves regarded as a classical age of literature, art and moral values. The Twelfth Dynasty, founded by Amenemhat I around 1985 BCE, was the strongest dynasty of the Middle Kingdom.

The Twelfth Dynasty, founded by Amenemhat I around 1985 BCE, was the strongest dynasty of the Middle Kingdom. Amenemhat moved the capital to a new city called Itjtawy, near the entrance to the Fayum, and reasserted royal control over the provinces by curbing the power of the nomarchs. He also introduced the practice of co-regency, in which a king would appoint his heir as co-ruler during his lifetime to ensure a smooth succession, a custom that was followed by many of his successors. The dynasty's kings undertook large-scale irrigation projects in the Fayum depression, turning the area into one of the most productive agricultural regions in the country.

The dynasty's kings undertook large-scale irrigation projects in the Fayum depression, turning the area into one of the most productive agricultural regions in the country. Senusret III, who ruled from about 1878 to 1839 BCE, is one of the most remarkable kings of the period. He conducted military campaigns in Nubia and built a chain of massive mud-brick fortresses, including Buhen and Semna, along

A History of Ancient Egypt Page 12 the second cataract of the Nile to control trade and mark the southern frontier. His portraits, which show a king with heavy-lidded eyes and a careworn face, broke with the idealised youthful look of earlier royal statues and convey a new sense of the burdens of kingship. Under his rule the powers of the provincial governors were reduced, and a larger and more professional bureaucracy emerged. The literature of the Middle Kingdom is regarded as the classical tradition of the Egyptian language, known as Middle Egyptian.

The literature of the Middle Kingdom is regarded as the classical tradition of the Egyptian language, known as Middle Egyptian. Works such as the Story of Sinuhe, the tale of an official who fled Egypt after the death of Amenemhat I and lived among the people of the Levant before returning home in old age, the Tale of the Eloquent Peasant, and the Instructions of Amenemhat are masterpieces of narrative and rhetoric. Scribes continued to copy and study these texts for centuries, and Middle Egyptian remained the language of monumental inscriptions until the end of pharaonic civilisation.

Scribes continued to copy and study these texts for centuries, and Middle Egyptian remained the language of monumental inscriptions until the end of pharaonic civilisation. The Thirteenth Dynasty, which followed the Twelfth, saw a rapid succession of short reigns, and central power weakened again. At the same time, Asiatic settlers who had been drawn to the eastern Delta by trade and opportunity gained increasing influence in the north. This slow disintegration set the stage for a new period of division and for the arrival of foreign rulers.

A History of Ancient Egypt Page 13 5. The Second Intermediate Period and the Rise of the New Kingdom Around 1650 BCE, the Egyptian state again broke up into smaller realms. A group of rulers of Canaanite origin, whom the Egyptians called Heqa-khasut, meaning rulers of foreign lands, and whom the Greeks later called the Hyksos, established control over the eastern Delta from their capital at Avaris, today's Tell el-Dab'a. The Hyksos are remembered in later Egyptian tradition as brutal invaders, but archaeological evidence suggests that they adopted many Egyptian customs, including hieroglyphic writing and royal titles, while also introducing new technologies.

The Hyksos are remembered in later Egyptian tradition as brutal invaders, but archaeological evidence suggests that they adopted many Egyptian customs, including hieroglyphic writing and royal titles, while also introducing new technologies. The horse-drawn chariot, the composite bow, improved bronze working and new types of fortifications appeared in Egypt in this period. Meanwhile a native Egyptian dynasty, the Seventeenth, maintained its rule from Thebes in the south, and a third power, the Kingdom of Kush, was emerging further south in Nubia. The Theban kings eventually challenged the Hyksos.

The Theban kings eventually challenged the Hyksos. An inscribed tablet records that Kamose, the last king of the Seventeenth Dynasty, was frustrated at sharing the country with an Asiatic ruler in the north and a Nubian ruler in the south, and he launched a campaign that brought Theban forces to the gates of Avaris. The mummy of Seqenenre Tao, Kamose's father or brother, bears wounds to the skull that suggest that he died in battle or was executed. The war of liberation was completed by Ahmose I, who expelled the Hyksos around 1550 BCE and reunified Egypt, founding the Eighteenth Dynasty and the New Kingdom.

The war of liberation was completed by Ahmose I, who expelled the Hyksos around 1550 BCE and reunified Egypt, founding the Eighteenth Dynasty and the New Kingdom. Ahmose also campaigned in Nubia and in the Levant, laying the foundation for the empire that his successors would build. The experience of foreign rule had a profound effect on Egyptian attitudes: the country now felt the need to create a buffer of territory around its borders, and the army, equipped with chariots and new weapons, became a major institution and a path to power for ambitious men.

The early kings of the Eighteenth Dynasty, Amenhotep I and Thutmose I, extended Egyptian control southward as far as the Fourth Cataract and

A History of Ancient Egypt Page 14 northeastward to the Euphrates. Thutmose I is also the first king known to have been buried in the Valley of the Kings, a hidden desert valley on the west bank at Thebes, rather than in a prominent pyramid that could be easily robbed. His tomb was cut deep into the rock, and its location was kept secret, while his mortuary temple was built separately on the edge of the cultivation. This separation of tomb and temple became standard for the next five centuries.

A History of Ancient Egypt Page 15 6. The New Kingdom: Egypt as an Imperial Power The New Kingdom, from about 1550 to 1069 BCE, was the era of Egypt's greatest power and wealth. Its monuments, such as the temples of Karnak and Luxor, the tombs of the Valley of the Kings and the colossal statues of Abu Simbel, are among the most famous in the world, and many of its rulers, including Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II, are household names. Egyptian armies campaigned in Nubia and Syria-Palestine, tribute poured into the treasury, and Thebes, home of the god Amun, became the religious capital of an empire.

Egyptian armies campaigned in Nubia and Syria-Palestine, tribute poured into the treasury, and Thebes, home of the god Amun, became the religious capital of an empire. Hatshepsut, the daughter of Thutmose I, ruled Egypt for about twenty years in the fifteenth century BCE. After the death of her husband Thutmose II she served first as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III, and then around 1473 BCE she assumed the full titles of a pharaoh, adopting royal regalia including the false beard and appearing in some statues in male form.

After the death of her husband Thutmose II she served first as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III, and then around 1473 BCE she assumed the full titles of a pharaoh, adopting royal regalia including the false beard and appearing in some statues in male form. Her reign was a time of peace and prosperity, and she is best known for her trading expedition to the Land of Punt, which is depicted in relief at her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari. The expedition returned with myrrh trees, ebony, ivory and exotic animals. After her death Thutmose III, and later perhaps his son, ordered many of her images to be removed or hacked out, though the motive remains debated.

Thutmose III is often called the Napoleon of Egypt because of his military successes. In a series of seventeen campaigns he extended Egyptian control to northern Syria, and his victory at the Battle of Megiddo, around 1457 BCE, against a coalition of Canaanite city-states led by the king of Kadesh, is the earliest battle in history for which a detailed account survives. The campaigns brought wealth, captives and tribute, and Egyptian influence reached its greatest geographical extent.

The campaigns brought wealth, captives and tribute, and Egyptian influence reached its greatest geographical extent. Under his successors, particularly Amenhotep III, who reigned from about 1390 to 1352 BCE, Egypt enjoyed unprecedented prosperity and diplomatic prestige, and the Amarna letters, a cache of clay tablets, show the king exchanging gifts and marriage alliances with the rulers of Babylon, Mitanni and Hatti.

A History of Ancient Egypt Page 16 The son of Amenhotep III, Amenhotep IV, initiated one of the most radical episodes in Egyptian history. In the fifth year of his reign he changed his name to Akhenaten, meaning effective for the Aten, and promoted the worship of the sun disc Aten above all other gods. He founded a new capital, Akhetaten, now known as Amarna, in Middle Egypt, and closed the temples of Amun. Art of the period, the Amarna style, is distinctive, with elongated skulls, slender limbs and intimate scenes of the royal family. His wife Nefertiti, whose painted limestone bust is one of the most recognised works of ancient art, appears in unusually prominent roles.

His wife Nefertiti, whose painted limestone bust is one of the most recognised works of ancient art, appears in unusually prominent roles. After Akhenaten's death the old religion was restored and Amarna was abandoned. The boy king Tutankhamun, who came to the throne at about the age of nine and died around 1323 BCE at about nineteen, would be a minor figure in history had his tomb not survived almost intact. The discovery of the tomb by Howard Carter in November 1922 revealed more than 5,000 objects, including the famous gold mask, golden shrines, chariots and jewellery.

The Nineteenth Dynasty saw a revival of imperial ambitions under Seti I and especially his son Ramesses II, called Ramesses the Great, who ruled for sixty-six years from about 1279 to 1213 BCE.

The Nineteenth Dynasty saw a revival of imperial ambitions under Seti I and especially his son Ramesses II, called Ramesses the Great, who ruled for sixty-six years from about 1279 to 1213 BCE. Ramesses fought the Hittites at the Battle of Kadesh around 1274 BCE, a clash of perhaps five thousand chariots that ended inconclusively although the king proclaimed it as a triumph on temple walls throughout Egypt. Some fifteen years later he concluded a peace treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III, the earliest surviving international peace treaty, a copy of which is displayed at the United Nations headquarters.

The Late Period, Persian Rule and the Ptolemies The centuries after the New Kingdom, known as the Third Intermediate Period, from about 1069 to 664 BCE, were marked by political division. Kings of the Twenty-First Dynasty ruled from Tanis in the Delta, while the high priests of Amun held power in Thebes. Later dynasties were founded by Libyan chieftains, descendants of soldiers who had settled in Egypt, and Shoshenq I, the first king of the Twenty-Second Dynasty, is probably the Shishak of the Bible who campaigned in Palestine around 925 BCE. By the eighth century BCE, Egypt was split among several competing rulers.

By the eighth century BCE, Egypt was split among several competing rulers. In this fragmented landscape, the Kingdom of Kush in Nubia, with its capital at Napata, grew in strength. King Piye marched northward around 727 BCE and brought most of Egypt under his control, founding the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty, also called the Kushite or Nubian dynasty. The Kushite pharaohs, among them Shabaka, Taharqa and Tanutamun, saw themselves as restorers of Egyptian tradition, and they built temples and revived the pyramid as a royal tomb in Nubia. Cloud Computing: Core Concepts 1.1 What cloud computing means Cloud computing is a model for providing on-demand access to shared computing resources—such as servers, storage, databases, networking, analytics, and software—over a network. Resources can be provisioned quickly and released when they are no longer needed. Instead of purchasing every server in advance, an organization can obtain capacity from a provider and pay according to its usage or subscription. A useful working definition has five characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service.

On-demand self-service means a customer can provision a resource without waiting for a provider employee to perform each step. Broad network access means services are reachable through standard network mechanisms from suitable clients. Resource pooling means provider resources serve multiple customers while maintaining logical separation. Rapid elasticity means capacity can expand or contract as demand changes. Measured service means usage is monitored and can be metered.

Measured service means usage is monitored and can be metered. 1.2 Service models Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) supplies fundamental computing resources such as virtual machines, networks, and disks. The customer generally manages the operating system, middleware, applications, and data. Amazon EC2 is a common AWS example. Platform as a Service (PaaS) provides a managed environment for deploying applications while the provider handles more of the underlying platform. Software as a Service (SaaS) delivers a complete application to end users; the customer usually configures the application rather than managing its servers. The labels are useful but not absolute. Early methods such as VITON predict a coarse try -on image from a person representation and the clothing item and then refine it [18]. Progress was limited by data: public datasets concentrated on upper-body garments at low resolution. Dress Code addressed this with 53, 795 image pairs at 1024 × 768 pixels in three categories, upper body, lower body and dresses [26], which are the garment categories of a fashion shop. 43 6. Discussion 6.1 Interpretation of the Compatibility Results The most informative result is a negative one. After rebalancing, the dual -path network reached 0.789 test accuracy but remained well below the linear model (0.932), and the validation sweep gave the linear model full weight. Three observations explain this. First, the labelled set is small: 948 training pairs cannot support a network with a six-figure parameter count, which is the memorisation-versus-generalisation trade-off that motivated wide- and-deep models [9].

First, the labelled set is small: 948 training pairs cannot support a network with a six-figure parameter count, which is the memorisation-versus-generalisation trade-off that motivated wide- and-deep models [9]. Second, the metadata -only model (0.928) is almost as accurate as the linear model with visual features (0.932), which suggests that the proxy labels depend mainly on category and colour. High accuracy therefore reflects, in part, the model recovering its own labelling rule rather than independent knowledge of what people consider well matched.

High accuracy therefore reflects, in part, the model recovering its own labelling rule rather than independent knowledge of what people consider well matched. Third, the visual signal alone is informative (0.705) but weaker, so a deep visual branch has little to add until more or better labels are available. For this reason the accuracy figures should be read as evidence that the pipeline learns what the labels encode, not as evidence about shopper taste. 6.2 Stability and Design Choices The weight-sensitivity analysis shows that the identity of the top five outfits depends on the balance between relevance and compatibility.

Solar Photovoltaic Energy: A Technical Reference Page 5 2. The Physics of the Photovoltaic Effect A solar cell is essentially a large-area semiconductor diode. When photons with energy greater than the semiconductor's band gap strike the material, they excite electrons from the valence band to the conduction band, creating electron–hole pairs. The built-in electric field at the p–n junction separates these carriers: electrons move toward the n-type side and holes toward the p-type side, producing a current when an external circuit is connected. Crystalline silicon has a band gap of 1.12 eV, which corresponds to a wavelength of about 1,110 nm in the near infrared.

Crystalline silicon has a band gap of 1.12 eV, which corresponds to a wavelength of about 1,110 nm in the near infrared. Photons with lower energy pass through the cell without being absorbed, while photons with much higher energy lose their excess energy as heat. These two loss mechanisms together limit the theoretical efficiency of a single-junction cell. The Shockley–Queisser limit predicts a maximum of about 33.7% for an ideal single-junction cell with a band gap near 1.34 eV, and about 29.4% for silicon specifically. 2.1 Doping and the p–n junction Pure silicon is an intrinsic semiconductor with few free carriers.

2.1 Doping and the p–n junction Pure silicon is an intrinsic semiconductor with few free carriers. Doping with phosphorus (a group V element) adds extra electrons and creates n-type material, while doping with boron (a group III element) creates p-type material with an excess of holes. Where the two regions meet, carriers diffuse across the boundary and leave behind fixed ionised atoms, forming a depletion region with a built-in potential of roughly 0.6–0.7 V in silicon. 2.2 The current–voltage characteristic The electrical behaviour of a cell is described by its I–V curve.

2.2 The current–voltage characteristic The electrical behaviour of a cell is described by its I–V curve. The short-circuit current (Isc) is the current when the terminals are shorted, and the open-circuit voltage (Voc) is the voltage when no current flows. The maximum power point (MPP) is the point on the curve where the product of current and voltage is greatest. The fill factor (FF) is the ratio of the maximum power to the product of Isc and Voc, and good silicon cells reach fill factors of 80–84%.
